A gene list becomes biologically useful when it is reorganized into processes: immune activation, immune restraint, epithelial cohesion, damage sensing, and escape from cell-cycle control. Reactome helps with that reorganization because it represents curated reactions and pathway hierarchies rather than associations inferred from co-expression alone [@milacic2024reactome]. But it also exposes an important limitation: several of the most interesting methylation candidates are poorly characterized and do not yet have direct curated Reactome pathways.

::: {.callout-note title="What this analysis is—and is not"}
The Reactome mappings were queried on 25 August 2026 with HGNC symbols, projection to human, and **interactors disabled**. The disease-stage scores below are qualitative hypotheses synthesized from the cited tissue literature; they are not patient measurements, differential-expression results, or pathway-enrichment p-values.
:::

## The 14-gene panel

The panel combines immune genes that were reported as hypomethylated in severe UC (**CD86, IL10, NLRC4, NLRP3, SIGLEC5, CLMP**) with promoter-hypermethylated or neoplasia-marker candidates (**FAM217B, KIAA1614, RIBC2, FOXE1, SYNE1**) and established epithelial/cancer-relevant genes (**CDH1, CDKN2A, GDNF**) [@kang2016ucpanel; @papadia2014foxesyne; @saito2011ucmethylation]. These are not interchangeable signals: some are pathway components, some are tissue markers, and some remain mechanistically under-annotated.


## Reactome coverage is uneven—and informative

Direct queries returned curated neighborhoods for nine genes. Examples include CD28/CTLA-4 and IL-10 signaling for CD86; CDH1 transcription, translation, and adherens-junction organization; oncogene- and oxidative-stress-induced senescence for CDKN2A; RET/NCAM signaling for GDNF; the IPAF inflammasome for NLRC4; the NLRP3 inflammasome; and neutrophil degranulation for SIGLEC5. SYNE1 mapped to meiotic synapsis, a real annotation but not an obvious colon mechanism. CLMP, FAM217B, FOXE1, KIAA1614, and RIBC2 were not directly mapped by this identifier analysis.

@fig-coverage makes that asymmetry visible. “Limited” does not mean unimportant: it means the database does not support a direct reaction-level bridge for the submitted symbol under these settings.

::: {#cell-fig-coverage .cell fig-height='7' fig-width='10' execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10,7))
sns.heatmap(M, cmap=sns.color_palette(["#F7FAFC",teal],as_cmap=True), cbar=False,
            linewidths=1,linecolor="white",square=False,ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Pathway neighborhood",ylabel="Candidate gene")
ax.tick_params(axis="x",rotation=0); ax.tick_params(axis="y",rotation=0)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"reactome-coverage.png",dpi=220,bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
```

Filled cells denote a curated direct pathway neighborhood or, for the final column, limited/absent direct mapping; assignments to biological modules are conservative.](index_files/figure-html/fig-coverage-output-1.png){#fig-coverage width=938 height=657}

## A network with three biological bridges

The central insight is not a single enriched pathway. It is a set of bridges between otherwise distinct programs, shown in @fig-reactome-network:

- **IL10–CD86** links immune restraint to antigen-presenting-cell co-stimulation. Reactome’s IL-10 pathway explicitly includes suppression of CD80/CD86 and pro-inflammatory cytokines [@milacic2024reactome].
- **NLRP3/NLRC4–SIGLEC5** places inflammasome outputs beside myeloid activation and inhibitory sialic-acid sensing. This is a functional neighborhood, not a claim that the three proteins form one complex.
- **CDH1–CDKN2A** connects epithelial architecture to the decision between repair, senescence, and clonal expansion. In UC tissue, both loci have inflammation- or neoplasia-associated methylation evidence [@wheeler2001cdh1; @hsieh1998p16].

::: {#cell-fig-reactome-network .cell fig-height='8' fig-width='12' execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,8)); ax.set(xlim=(-6,6),ylim=(-4.5,4.5)); ax.axis("off")
mod_pos={"Immune regulation":(-3.7,2.7),"Inflammasomes":(0,3.2),"Barrier / adhesion":(3.7,2.7),
         "Trophic signaling":(-3.7,-2.5),"Senescence":(0,-3.1),"Under-annotated":(3.7,-2.5)}
gene_groups={"Immune regulation":["IL10","CD86","SIGLEC5"],"Inflammasomes":["NLRP3","NLRC4"],
 "Barrier / adhesion":["CDH1","CLMP"],"Trophic signaling":["GDNF"],"Senescence":["CDKN2A"],
 "Under-annotated":["FAM217B","KIAA1614","RIBC2","FOXE1","SYNE1"]}
gene_pos={}
for mod,(mx,my) in mod_pos.items():
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((mx-1.3,my-.42),2.6,.84,boxstyle="round,pad=.08",fc=navy,ec="none"))
    ax.text(mx,my,mod,ha="center",va="center",color="white",weight="bold")
    gs=gene_groups[mod]
    span = 2.0 if mod=="Under-annotated" else 1.0
    offsets=np.linspace(-span,span,len(gs)) if len(gs)>1 else [0]
    for off,g in zip(offsets,gs):
        gx=mx+off; gy=my-1.15 if my>0 else my+1.15; gene_pos[g]=(gx,gy)
        col=gray if mod=="Under-annotated" else teal
        width = .92 if mod=="Under-annotated" else 1.1
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((gx-width/2,gy-.25),width,.5,boxstyle="round,pad=.05",fc=col,ec="white"))
        ax.text(gx,gy,g,ha="center",va="center",color="white",weight="bold",fontsize=8 if mod=="Under-annotated" else 9)
        ax.plot([mx,gx],[my-.45 if my>0 else my+.45,gy+.27 if my>0 else gy-.27],color=col,lw=1.8)
bridges=[("Immune regulation","Inflammasomes","immune restraint / activation"),
         ("Inflammasomes","Barrier / adhesion","pyroptosis · permeability"),
         ("Barrier / adhesion","Senescence","injury · repair · selection"),
         ("Senescence","Under-annotated","methylation markers"),
         ("Trophic signaling","Barrier / adhesion","survival · tissue repair")]
for a,b,label in bridges:
    x1,y1=mod_pos[a]; x2,y2=mod_pos[b]
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x1,y1),(x2,y2),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=14,
                                  linestyle="--",color=coral,lw=1.8,connectionstyle="arc3,rad=.08",shrinkA=55,shrinkB=55))
    ax.text((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2+.18,label,ha="center",fontsize=8,color=coral,
            bbox=dict(fc="white",ec="none",alpha=.8,pad=1))
ax.text(0,4.15,"Curated neighborhoods connected by disease-level hypotheses",ha="center",weight="bold",fontsize=14,color=navy)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"reactome-network.png",dpi=220,bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
```

Solid links are direct curated pathway memberships; dashed links are disease-level bridges proposed for colitis-to-cancer interpretation, not direct molecular reactions.](index_files/figure-html/fig-reactome-network-output-1.png){#fig-reactome-network width=1137 height=753}

## What is likely to be visible at each disease stage?

The pathway signal expected in a biopsy depends on both regulation and cell composition. Active colitis should most strongly expose innate sensing, leukocyte co-regulation, epithelial junction disruption, and compensatory IL-10. Long-standing colitis can add senescence and methylation-field signals. Established cancer may retain inflammatory circuitry while making cell-cycle escape and epithelial plasticity more prominent. @fig-stage-map is a qualitative expectation map, not a measured heatmap.

::: {#cell-fig-stage-map .cell fig-height='5.5' fig-width='9' execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
stage = pd.DataFrame({
 "Healthy colon":[1,0,3,0,2,0],
 "Active colitis":[3,3,1,2,2,1],
 "Long-standing UC":[2,2,1,3,1,2],
 "Colitis-associated CRC":[2,1,0,3,1,3]}, index=["Immune co-regulation","Inflammasome activity","Barrier integrity","Senescence / escape","Trophic signaling","Candidate methylation markers"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9,5.5))
sns.heatmap(stage,cmap=sns.light_palette(coral,as_cmap=True),vmin=0,vmax=3,annot=True,fmt="d",linewidths=1,linecolor="white",cbar_kws={"label":"Hypothesized prominence"},ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Disease context",ylabel="Pathway program")
ax.tick_params(axis="x",rotation=18); ax.tick_params(axis="y",rotation=0)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(OUT/"reactome-stage-map.png",dpi=220,bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Qualitative hypotheses for pathway visibility across disease states. Scores encode expected relative prominence (0–3), not observed expression or clinical effect size.](index_files/figure-html/fig-stage-map-output-1.png){#fig-stage-map width=830 height=511}
:::
:::


## Gene-by-gene Reactome reading

| Gene | Direct Reactome neighborhood from the query | Colitis/CRC interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **CD86** | IL-10 signaling; CD28 Vav1 and PI3K/AKT; CTLA-4 co-inhibition | APC abundance and immune context; not a unidirectional activation marker |
| **CDH1** | CDH1 transcription/translation; type-I cadherins; adherens junctions | Barrier architecture, epithelial plasticity, and methylation-associated silencing |
| **CDKN2A** | Oncogene- and oxidative-stress-induced senescence | Stress arrest in colitis; loss can permit neoplastic escape |
| **CLMP** | No direct mapping in this query | Strong developmental intestinal genetics, uncertain adult UC pathway [@rathjen2023clmp] |
| **FAM217B** | No direct mapping | UC methylation candidate; mechanism unknown [@kang2016ucpanel] |
| **FOXE1** | No direct mapping | Neoplasia-associated methylation marker; colon driver role unproven [@papadia2014foxesyne] |
| **GDNF** | RET signaling; NCAM1 interactions and neurite outgrowth | Trophic stromal/neural signaling; inflammation-associated methylation [@saito2011ucmethylation] |
| **IL10** | IL-10 production/signaling neighborhoods | Compensatory immune brake; ligand abundance does not prove response [@glocker2009il10r] |
| **KIAA1614** | No direct mapping | UC promoter-methylation candidate with predicted, not established, polarity biology |
| **NLRC4** | IPAF/NLRC4 inflammasome | Bacterial invasion sensing after barrier breach |
| **NLRP3** | NLRP3 inflammasome | DAMP and organelle-stress sensing; activation requires more than RNA or methylation |
| **RIBC2** | No direct mapping | Cilia biology in *Xenopus*; colon relevance unresolved [@chung2014ribc2] |
| **SIGLEC5** | Neutrophil degranulation; immunoregulatory interactions | Myeloid abundance and inhibitory/activating paired-Siglec balance |
| **SYNE1** | Meiotic synapsis in this query | The colon signal is more defensible as a methylation biomarker than this pathway mapping |

## The most useful experimental panel

The graph suggests measuring pathway outputs rather than adding more isolated genes. In paired tissue and plasma, a compact follow-up panel could combine:

1. epithelial fraction, membrane E-cadherin, and permeability;
2. NLRP3/NLRC4 complexes, cleaved caspase-1, gasdermin D, IL-1β, and IL-18;
3. CD86-positive APC abundance, IL-10 protein, and IL-10-induced phospho-STAT3;
4. p16^INK4a^/p14^ARF^ promoter-specific methylation, RNA, protein, and RB/p53 state;
5. exact CpGs for FAM217B, KIAA1614, RIBC2, FOXE1, and SYNE1, validated in an external cohort.

That design keeps three questions separate: **Which cells are present? Which pathways are active? Which methylation changes add predictive information?** Reactome is strongest for the second question. It cannot, by itself, convert an under-characterized methylation marker into a mechanism.
